The twin never sees a brief, an opinion or a news story. It sees a case packet: the question presented (verbatim from the Court), the lower court’s holding, the procedural posture and three arguments per side, assembled from the public record before argument and checked by a person so that nothing in it reveals an outcome. The next block sets CASE, loads that packet and prints it. Change CASE to "johnson" for the live case.
Text 1.1. The case packet for CASE, as the twin receives it.

CASE <- "landor"

packet <- paste(readLines(file.path(DATA, paste0(CASE, "_packet.md")), warn = FALSE),
                collapse = "\n")
cat(packet)

# Case packet — Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections, No. 23-1197

**Argued:** 2025-11-10 · **Sitting:** October Term 2025 · **Packet author:** auto (Oyez pre-decision fields; verifier initials: ____) · **Packet date:** 2026-09-30
**Sources used:** Oyez case record — `question` and `facts_of_the_case` as published before argument; lower court from the record. *No brief, no opinion, no post-argument material.*
**Parties:** Petitioner: Damon Landor · Respondent: Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

## Question(s) presented (as summarised by Oyez; the Court's QP list governs if they differ)
1. May an individual sue a government official in his individual capacity for damages for violations of the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA)?

## Facts and lower court (Oyez pre-decision summary)
Damon Landor, a devout Rastafarian, vowed as part of his faith never to cut his hair—a religious commitment known as the Nazarite Vow. Incarcerated in 2020, Landor was first held at the St. Tammany Parish Detention Center and later at LaSalle Correctional Center, both of which allowed him to maintain his hairstyle in accordance with his religious beliefs. After approximately five months and with three weeks left in his sentence, Landor was transferred to Raymond Laborde Correctional Center. Upon arrival, Landor proactively explained his religious practices and presented documentation of previous accommodations, including a copy of a federal court decision supporting similar claims. An intake guard disregarded his documentation, summoned the warden, and upon Landor’s inability to produce immediate additional proof of his beliefs, guards forcibly handcuffed Landor and shaved his head.

Following his release, Landor sued the Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety, its Secretary James LeBlanc, the correctional center, and Warden Marcus Myers, asserting claims under the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) and 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for violations of his federal constitutional rights, as well as state law claims.

The U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Louisiana dismissed Landor’s individual-capacity RLUIPA claims for money damages, holding such relief unavailable under controlling Fifth Circuit precedent. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed, relying on its prior decision in Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas, and rejecting Landor’s arguments that subsequent Supreme Court authority or other legal developments altered that result.

Lower court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

## Procedural posture
Certiorari granted 2025-06-23; argued 2025-11-10.

The twin is told who it is, when and by whom it was appointed, and one number: the Justice’s Martin–Quinn score for October Term 2024, a statistical summary of their voting record on a scale where negative is liberal and positive is conservative. 3. The evidence
The twin does not get the Justice’s whole record. For each case it gets eight passages, retrieved from an index of that Justice’s own opinions (October Terms 1991 to 2024, about 37,000 passages across the nine) by three queries written from the packet: the question presented, the doctrinal area and precedents, and the two sides’ first arguments. The retrieval has rules: at least two passages from majority opinions and two from separate writings, at most two from any one earlier case, nothing from the case at issue, nothing after October Term 2024. The retrieval has already been done; the eight passages for JUSTICE on CASE are in the file you loaded, together with a hash of the set so the run can be reproduced.

in such a case says: “Although this official is immune from damages [ 563 U.S. 703 ]
today, what he did violates the Constitution and he or anyone else who does that thing
again will be personally liable.” If the official regularly engages in that conduct as
part of his job (as Camreta does), he suffers injury caused by the adverse constitutional

4. The prompt
The twin receives two messages. The system message says who it is, where its evidence comes from, and that the case is undecided. The user message carries the persona line, the eight passages with their context, the packet, and the task with the JSON format of the answer. The project builds both from a template whose hash is logged with every run; the text below is that build, exactly as sent.
The block below prints the system message.
Text 4.1. The system message.

cat(strwrap(tw$system, width = 90), sep = "\n")

You are a research instrument: a digital twin of Elena Kagan, Associate Justice of the
Supreme Court of the United States, built for a pre-registered study of whether justice
twins can anticipate votes on cases the Court has not yet decided.

You reason as Justice Kagan would, from two sources only: (1) the evidence below, which
consists of passages from opinions Justice Kagan wrote or co-wrote, with short
Reporter-prepared context on the earlier cases they come from, and (2) your general
knowledge of Justice Kagan's published jurisprudence up to the end of October Term 2024.
The case you are asked about has not been decided and you do not know its outcome; if you
believe you recall a decision in it, disregard that recollection and reason from the
record and the packet.

Answer in the JSON schema requested, and nothing else.


The user message is long because it carries the evidence. The next block prints its first sixty lines and its last thirty, which is where the persona and the task sit; the middle is the evidence you read in Section 3.
Text 4.2. The user message, head and tail.

u <- strsplit(tw$user, "\n")[[1]]
cat(head(u, 60), sep = "\n")

## Who you are

Elena Kagan, Associate Justice, appointed by President Barack Obama, on the Court since 2010.
Ideal point (Martin–Quinn, October Term 2024 posterior mean): -1.84, on a scale where negative values are liberal and positive values conservative; this term the nine justices ran from -4.19 to +3.07. Treat this as a coarse summary of voting tendency, not a rule.

## Evidence: your own prior writing

Each passage is from an opinion you wrote or co-wrote in an earlier case (term and opinion type in the header). Context blocks after the passages summarise those earlier cases; they are prepared by the Reporter of Decisions, not by you, and are provided so you know what each case was about.

He thus can demonstrate, as we demand, injury, causation, and redress-ability. 4 And conversely, if the person who initially brought the suit may again be subject to the challenged conduct, she has a stake in preserving the court’s holding. See Erie v. Pap’s *1131 A. M., 529 U.S. 277, 287-289 , 120 S. Ct. 1382 , 146 L. Ed. 2d 265 (2000); Honig v. Doe, 484 U.S. 305, 318-323 , 108 S. Ct. 592 , 98 L. Ed. 2d 686 (1988); cf. Lyons, 461 U.S., at 111 , 103 S. Ct. 1660 , 75 L. Ed. 2d 675 (examining whether the plaintiff had shown “a sufficient likelihood that he will again be wronged in a similar way”). Only if the ruling remains good law will she have ongoing protection from the practice.

That the victor has filed the appeal does not deprive us of jurisdiction. The parties in such cases may yet have a sufficient “interest in the outcome of [a litigated] issue” to present a case or controversy.

Nor will we create a freestanding exception to tribal immunity for all off-reservation commercial conduct. This Court has declined that course once before. To choose it now would entail both overthrowing our precedent and usurping Congress's current policy judgment. Accordingly, Michigan may not sue Bay Mills to enjoin the Vanderbilt casino, but must instead use available alternative means to accomplish that object.

 It is so ordered.

Nothing in § 2710(d)(7)(A)(ii) or any other provision of IGRA limits that grant of jurisdiction (although those provisions may indicate that a party has no statutory right of action). See Verizon Md. Inc. v. Public Serv. Comm'n of Md., 535 U.S. 635 , 643-644, 122 S.Ct. 1753 , 152 L.Ed.2d 871 (2002).

And under modern takings law, there is “no magic
formula” to determine “whether a given government interference with property is a taking.” Ibid. For that reason,
a government actor usually cannot know in advance
whether implementing a regulatory program will effect a
taking, much less of whose property. Until today, such an
official could do his work without fear of wrongdoing, in
any jurisdiction that had set up a reliable means for property owners to obtain compensation. Even if some regulatory action turned out to take someone’s property, the
official would not have violated the Constitution. But no
longer. Now, when a government undertakes land-use
regulation (and what government doesn’t?), the responsible employees will almost inescapably become constitutional malefactors. That is not a fair position in which to
place persons carrying out their governmental duties.
   Still more important, the majority’s ruling channels to
federal courts a (potentially massive) set of cases that
more properly belongs, at least in the first instance, in
state courts—where Williamson County put them. The
regulation of land use, this Court has stated, is “perhaps
the quintessential state activity.” FERC v. Mississippi,
456 U. S. 742, 768, n. 30 (1982). And a claim that a landuse regulation violates the Takings Clause usually turns
on state-law issues. In that respect, takings claims have
little in common with other constitutional challenges. The
question in takings cases is not merely whether a given
state action meets federal constitutional standards. Before those standards can come into play, a court must
typically decide whether, under state law, the plaintiff has
a property interest in the thing regulated. See Phillips v.
Washington Legal Foundation, 524 U. S. 156, 164 (1998);
see also Sterk, The Demise of Federal Takings Litigation,
48 Wm. & Mary L. Rev. 251, 288 (2006) (“[I]f background
state law did not recognize or create property in the first
instance, then a subsequent state action cannot take
property”). Often those questions—how does pre-existing
state law define the property right?; what interests does
that law grant?; and conversely what interests does it
deny?—are nuanced and complicated.

7. Change one thing
Everything above is one draw from one configuration. The question that matters for the method is which inputs the answer depends on. Pick one of the three changes below, re-run Section 5’s live block, and compare.

text:
8. What a twin cannot know
Three things to carry out of the room.
The twin only ever sees what is in Sections 1 to 4. Nothing from the term being predicted is in its evidence; the case at issue is excluded from retrieval by rule; the packet is checked by a person for anything that reveals an outcome. When the twins are right, it is for reasons you can read; when they are wrong, you can see what they were reading.
A prediction filed before argument is a prediction. The project’s October votes were filed on FantasySCOTUS on 4 October, each run logged with the hash of its packet, its evidence set, its prompt template and its model. The decisions come in the spring. Until then the numbers on the slide are the validation run on last term’s cases, where the answers are known, and nothing else.
And the obvious caveat: a model that has read the whole internet may remember a decided case however firmly it is told not to. That is exactly why the record is built on cases that are not yet decided.

4. The backtest
The test is simple. Every day, sort that day’s stocks on net_buy_share into five equal groups, quintiles: quintile 1 holds the fifth the twins liked least, quintile 5 the fifth they liked most. Then average the forward excess return within each quintile, day by day. If the twins know something, quintile 5 should beat quintile 1. The difference, quintile 5 minus quintile 1, is the return of a long–short portfolio: buy the favoured fifth, short the disfavoured fifth, so the market’s own movement cancels out.
The block below assigns the quintiles. Ties are broken at random, with a fixed seed so everyone gets the same answer.

set.seed(13)
events[, quintile := ceiling(5 * frank(net_buy_share, ties.method = "random") / .N),
       by = event_date]

title: Notebook 3 — MrP and validation
text:
Notebook 2 left you 400 interviewed twins. Each has a probability of voting for Harris in 2024 and for Brown in 2026. Averaging them tells you about these 400 twins. MrP (multilevel regression and post-stratification) turns them into an estimate for Ohio, and for each of its 15 districts:

regress: fit a multilevel model with the twin’s answer on the left and who the twin is on the right. In words: P(Harris), or P(Brown), modelled on sex, degree, age band, ethnicity and district;
post-stratify: predict every cell of the Ohio frame and add the cells up, weighted by how many people the frame puts in each;

You will fit two versions. Model A is textbook census MrP and fails at the district level in an instructive way. Model B uses the stage-2 frame from Notebook 1 and gets the districts right, for a reason you should be suspicious of.
The last section steps back from your 400 twins to the Talking to Machines panels: twelve of them, and a held-out election that tests what the 2024 recall cannot.

title: Notebook 3 — MrP and validation
text:
3. Model A: census MrP
The outcome is each twin’s Harris probability among 2024 voters. The probability comes from the interview in Notebook 2: each twin answered with probabilities rather than a choice, so it enters the model as a fractional Harris vote and a fractional Trump vote. In practice every twin enters twice: once as a Harris vote with weight p, once as a Trump vote with weight 1 − p. A logistic model fitted to these rows estimates the same thing as a model of the probabilities themselves. glmer warns about non-integer weights, which is expected here.
Model A is the textbook MrP: it uses only what the census knows about people.

Fixed effects for the two-level variables, sex and degree.
Random intercepts for age, ethnicity and district. A district with few twins is pulled towards the state average; one with more is left closer to its own data. This partial pooling is the “multilevel” in MrP.

The block below prints nothing. It defines stack(), which makes the two rows per twin (y = 1 weighted by p, y = 0 weighted by 1 − p), applies it to voters to build the model’s data, s24, and defines fit(), the one call that fits every model in this notebook.

stack <- function(d, p, w = rep(1, nrow(d))) {
  keep <- d[, .(cd, gender, ethnicity, age_bins, college_grad, vote2024)]
  rbind(cbind(keep, y = 1L, wt = p * w), cbind(keep, y = 0L, wt = (1 - p) * w))
}
s24 <- stack(voters, voters$harris_2p)

# one fitting call for every model in this notebook; nAGQ = 0 is the fast, robust approximation
fit <- function(f, d) suppressWarnings(glmer(f, data = d, weights = wt, family = binomial, nAGQ = 0))

The next block fits Model A as m_a, prints how long it took, and prints the standard deviation of each random intercept.
Table 3.5. Model A: the random-intercept standard deviations (Std.Dev.), one per grouping.

m_a <- fit(y ~ gender + college_grad + (1 | age_bins) + (1 | ethnicity) + (1 | cd), s24)
cat(sprintf("fitted in %.1f s\n", as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "secs"))))

Post-stratify
Predict every frame cell, including cells no twin sits in (allow.new.levels gives them the average for that group). Then weight each cell by its 2024 voters, and add up.

5. Model B: put the vote class back
Your frame already knows each cell’s 2024 politics. Stage 2 (Notebook 1, Section 2) split every cell into D, R, other and stay-home, raked to the certified result. Every twin carries its class, and the donor was matched on it. Model B adds the class as a predictor and post-stratifies over cell × vote class, using the stage-2 counts.
Be clear about the mechanism before you look at the result. The new predictor is the 2024 vote class of the twin’s cell, which was raked to the certified result. The outcome is the twin’s own 2024 answer, and the twin’s donor was chosen to share that same class. So the model regresses the twins’ 2024 answers on a variable those answers were built to follow. each cell’s D and R counts were raked to that very result (Notebook 1, Section 2);
each twin’s donor was matched on the class of its cell (Notebook 2, Section 3);
so the donated attitudes the model read were chosen to fit that class, and the model gave the class back almost every time (Notebook 2, Table 2.12);
Model B then weights those answers by the same raked class counts.

Recovering 2024 therefore tests whether the pipeline kept what it was given. It says nothing about whether the twins can read an election. That is worth knowing, since a pipeline that lost its inputs would be broken, but it is a check on the plumbing. A recovery within a point or two is the pipeline working as designed.
Evidence that twins can read an election needs an election that is in no part of the pipeline: not in the frame, the rake, the donors or the persona. If the twins get that one right, the calibration cannot be the reason. Section 7 has one: New Jersey, November 2025.

6. The 2026 Senate race
For 2026, Model B’s structure is the useful one. It asks how each 2024 class, within each census cell, votes in 2026, and weights the cells by the frame’s class counts. It needs two models, because who turns out is not given:

a turnout model, fitted on every twin (the probability of voting at all);
a vote model on Brown’s two-party share, with each twin weighted by its own probability of voting.

Your twins have no third-party class, so the vote class enters as a random intercept. The frame’s small “Other” class (51,202 adults in Table 3.3, about 0.6% of Ohio) then gets the average.
The block below prints nothing. It adds two columns to iv: turnout (one minus the no_vote probability) and brown_2p (Brown’s share of the Brown + Husted probability). It fits the turnout model (m_turn) and the vote model (m_vote), and adds both predictions to every row of frame_class (p_turn, p_brown). brown_state is Brown’s share among expected voters in Ohio, and turnout_state the expected turnout among adults.

iv[, `:=`(turnout = 1 - no_vote, brown_2p = dem / (dem + rep))]
f26 <- y ~ gender + college_grad + (1 | vote2024) + (1 | age_bins) + (1 | ethnicity) + (1 | cd)
m_turn <- fit(f26, stack(iv, iv$turnout))
m_vote <- fit(f26, stack(iv, iv$brown_2p, iv$turnout))
frame_class[, `:=`(p_turn  = predict(m_turn, newdata = frame_class, type = "response", allow.new.levels = TRUE),
                   p_brown = predict(m_vote, newdata = frame_class, type = "response", allow.new.levels = TRUE))]
brown_state   <- frame_class[, sum(N * p_turn * p_brown) / sum(N * p_turn)]
turnout_state <- frame_class[, sum(N * p_turn) / sum(N)]

title: Notebook 3 — MrP and validation
text:
What to take away

MrP is what turns 400 twins into Ohio, but only as well as the frame knows what matters. A census-only frame knows demographics. Ohio’s districts differ politically, so census MrP shrinks them together.
Recovering 2024 is not validation. The stage-2 frame and the donor match were both calibrated to it, so Model B gets it right largely by construction.
A record-only twin is a stable partisan baseline. It does not know the 2026 environment, and the gap to the polls is the size of that environment.
The structure is real; the level needs care. Geography holds up on an election the twins never saw. Level accuracy in any one election depends on knowing both the panel’s baseline bias and the swing.

title: Notebook 3 — MrP and validation
text:
Where this comes from
The twelve panels and the New Jersey held-out test come from the digital-twin work of Talking to Machines, an international collaboration of academics and industry researchers directed by Sonja Vogt (HEC Lausanne) and Ray Duch (Nuffield College, Oxford).

title: Notebook 1 — Building a silicon sample
text:
A digital twin is not a random person. It is a slot in a measured population frame, filled by a record and then given attitudes by a matched survey respondent. This notebook builds the frame and fills 400 of those slots for Ohio, then audits what you drew.
By the end you will have:

read a stage-1 frame — who lives in each Ohio district, from the ACS;
read a stage-2 frame — how each of those cells voted in November 2024;
checked the frame against the certified 2024 result;
collapsed it to a teaching mini-frame;
drawn 400 synthetic skeletons by probability-proportional-to-size sampling;
audited the drawn margins, and raked them to the acceptance standard.

Nothing here calls a language model. That is the point: the composition of a panel is fixed by census and certified-result data before any model is involved. The model never chooses who is in the panel.

A note on what you are drawing. There are two routes to a skeleton. The stronger one starts from a state voter file: the official list of registered voters, with each person’s county, registration and turnout history. Ohio publishes one, and the Talking to Machines panel draws real registrants from it into these cells. Working with a voter file requires a licence and ethical care, because every row is a real, identifiable person. This notebook takes the other route: it draws synthetic skeletons directly from the census frame. Section 7 shows what the registrant route adds.

How to read this notebook. Every table and figure the code prints has a number (Table 1.1, Figure 1.1, …), given in bold just above the code that prints it. When the text quotes a number, it says which table it comes from, and which row or column to look at.
The first block loads the three R packages the notebook uses and fixes the random seed, so everyone draws the same panel.

set.seed(20261013L)   # every draw in this notebook is seeded and reproducible

text:
4. The mini-frame
The project’s registrant draw uses district × county × sex × ethnicity × age as its cell key, with the vote class assigned inside each cell. County is not in the ACS frame — it enters only from the voter file, which splits each frame cell across counties by its own composition. Since you are drawing synthetically, your key is:
district × sex × ethnicity × age × college × vote2024
The mini-frame is not a subset. It holds the same citizen adults as sf2, under a different key: the vote class moves from four count columns (N_D, N_R, N_Other, N_stay) into the key, and household income drops out. Same people, re-keyed.
Why can a synthetic draw not have county? The ACS does not publish it. The smallest geography in the PUMS is the PUMA, and PUMAs and counties do not nest: a rural PUMA combines several whole counties, and an urban county is split across several PUMAs. Placing a synthetic person in a county would mean inventing that joint distribution. A voter file records each registrant’s county directly.
This is worth pausing on. Leaving county out is a real defect. When the project’s panels were drawn without it, a county’s realised partisan composition was an uncontrolled by-product of the draw, and Passaic County, New Jersey came out 13.4 points too Democratic. Adding county to the cell key brought the state’s county error from 2.98 to 1.73 points. Your synthetic sample cannot have this control, and it is the clearest illustration of what a voter file buys you.
The block below builds the mini-frame as a table called mini. It turns each sf2 row into four rows, one per vote class, each with that class’s count as its N; drops the empty ones; adds up rows that now share the same key (which is where income disappears); and sorts them. It prints the number of cells and people, then the first five rows.

text:
5. Draw 400 skeletons
Systematic probability-proportional-to-size. Sort the cells, take the cumulative population, lay down 400 equally spaced points along it, and take the cell each point lands in. Compared with drawing 400 independent cells this gives margins on the leading sort keys that are exact to ±1 — which is why the project’s draw uses it.
The block below writes that procedure as a function, draw_pps(), and runs it on mini to draw 400 skeletons into a table called panel. Inside the function: step is the population between two picks; start is a random point inside the first step; picks are the 400 equally spaced points; cum is the running total of N down the sorted cells; and findInterval() finds the cell each point lands in. Each pick gets an id, oh_syn_0001 to oh_syn_0400. The block prints the size of panel and its first five rows.
Table 1.7. panel, your 400 skeletons: size, then the first five.

draw_pps <- function(frame, n, seed = 20261013L) {
  set.seed(seed)
  f    <- copy(frame)[N > 0]
  step <- sum(f$N) / n
  start <- runif(1, 0, step)
  picks <- start + step * (0:(n - 1))
  f[, cum := cumsum(N)]
  idx  <- findInterval(picks, c(0, f$cum), rightmost.closed = TRUE)
  out  <- f[idx]
  out[, `:=`(cum = NULL, N = NULL)]
  out[, twin_id := sprintf("oh_syn_%04d", seq_len(.N))]
  setcolorder(out, "twin_id")
  out[]
}

Read Table 1.8 from left to right. 8,931,251 people over 400 picks is one pick every 22,328 people (people_per_pick). The cells are sorted, their populations added up into a running total, the first point falls at random inside the first 22,328, and each later point is one step further on. 6. Audit what you drew
A panel is only useful if it is the electorate in miniature. The project’s acceptance standard is: every one-way margin within 0.3 percentage points unweighted, and 0.00 weighted, with no cell short.
A one-way margin is the share of the panel in each category of one variable: the share that is female, the share in each age band, and so on. The audit compares your panel with the mini-frame. The mini-frame is sf2 re-keyed, so its one-way margins are the full frame’s: this is your panel against the Ohio frame.
The block below writes the comparison as a function, margin_check(). For one variable it computes the share of panel in each category (panel_share), the share of mini’s people in the same category (frame_share), and the difference in points (diff_pp). It then runs it for the five audited variables and prints only the largest gap for each.
Table 1.10. The audit, largest gap per variable (in percentage points).

margin_check <- function(panel, frame, var) {
  p <- panel[, .(panel_share = .N / nrow(panel)), by = var]
  f <- frame[, .(frame_share = sum(N) / sum(frame$N)), by = var]
  m <- merge(p, f, by = var, all = TRUE)
  m[is.na(panel_share), panel_share := 0][is.na(frame_share), frame_share := 0]
  m[, diff_pp := 100 * (panel_share - frame_share)]
  m[order(-abs(diff_pp))]
}

for (v in c("gender", "ethnicity", "age_bins", "vote2024", "cd")) {

      sprintf("%.2f pp\n", max(abs(margin_check(panel, mini, v)$diff_pp))))

Raking the residual away
Systematic PPS leaves rounding residue on the margins that are not the leading sort key. Raking removes it: each skeleton gets a weight, and the weights are adjusted one variable at a time, round after round, until the weighted shares match the frame’s.
The block below defines three functions: rake() computes the weights; wmargin() is the weighted version of the margin check; report() prints the range of the weights and the largest weighted gap for each variable. It then rakes panel on the five variables, stores the result in a new column, weight, and prints the report.
Table 1.13. The raked 400-skeleton panel: weight range, then the largest weighted gap per variable.

rake <- function(panel, frame, vars, iters = 50) {
  w <- rep(1, nrow(panel))
  for (i in seq_len(iters)) {
    for (v in vars) {
      tgt <- frame[, .(t = sum(N) / sum(frame$N)), by = v]
      cur <- data.table(lvl = panel[[v]], w = w)[, .(c = sum(w)), by = lvl][, c := c / sum(c)]
      setnames(cur, "lvl", v)
      f <- merge(cur, tgt, by = v)[, ratio := t / c]
      w <- w * f$ratio[match(panel[[v]], f[[v]])]
    }
  }
  w / mean(w)
}

MARGINS <- c("gender", "ethnicity", "age_bins", "vote2024", "cd")

wmargin <- function(panel, frame, var) {
  p <- panel[, .(panel_share = sum(weight) / sum(panel$weight)), by = var]
  f <- frame[, .(frame_share = sum(N) / sum(frame$N)), by = var]
  merge(p, f, by = var, all = TRUE)[is.na(panel_share), panel_share := 0
    ][, max(abs(100 * (panel_share - frame_share)))]
}

report <- function(panel, frame, label) {
  cat(label, sprintf("— weights %.2f–%.2f\n", min(panel$weight), max(panel$weight)))
  for (v in MARGINS)
    cat(sprintf("   %-10s weighted max |diff| = %.4f pp\n", v, wmargin(panel, frame, v)))
}

title: Notebook 2 — Personas and the digital interview
text:
Notebook 1 gave you 400 skeletons: slots in the Ohio frame with a district, a sex, an age, an ethnicity, a degree and a 2024 vote class, and nothing else. A skeleton cannot be interviewed. This notebook gives each one a voice and then asks it how it votes.
By the end you will have:

matched every skeleton to a real survey respondent: an Ohio respondent to the Cooperative Election Study (CES), 2020–2025;
rendered each twin as a persona, the text record the model reads;
interviewed the panel with the Talking to Machines vote module;
aggregated the answers and checked them against the certified 2024 result and the 2026 Senate polls.



Figure 2.1. How one twin is built (A), and the three panels compared in Section 6 (B).









A twin is a skeleton plus a donor, written out as one block of text called a persona. The skeleton says who the person is: one cell of the census frame, drawn in Notebook 1. The donor says what they think: one real CES respondent, matched to the skeleton. Neither is a twin on its own.
A civic record is what a state voter file records about a registrant: their county, the year they registered, which general elections they voted in, and which primary ballot they last took. A registrant twin carries one. Yours carries an empty one, because a synthetic skeleton has no voter-file row behind it, and the persona says “not observed” rather than inventing it.
Three panels, with fixed names. Section 6 compares three things, and this notebook keeps their names throughout:

your panel: 400 synthetic twins, built and interviewed here;
the project’s panel: 4,000 real registrants from the Ohio voter file, with the same donors, persona template and vote module;
the benchmark: the certified 2024 result and the 2026 polling average.

Panels 1 and 2 differ only in where the skeleton comes from, so the gap between them is what a voter file buys. Neither panel was fitted to the 2026 figure.

Where the attitudes come from. The skeleton fixes who the twin is. Its values, issue positions, circumstances and media diet are donated by the matched respondent, and the persona says so line by line. The model is given this whole record and asked how this person would vote. It is not asked to make a person up.

3. Hot-deck matching
Each skeleton is matched to a donor in its own cell, on five nested keys. The algorithm tries the finest key first and falls back only when the cell holds fewer than five donors:



Level
Key

Age band and ethnicity are in every key, so they always match. The vote class drops out only at levels 4 and 5. Within a cell the donor is drawn at random.
The block below writes the five keys as functions (K) and the matching as a function, hotdeck(). For each skeleton, hotdeck() looks for donors with the same level-1 key; if there are at least five (THIN_CELL), it draws one at random, and otherwise it tries level 2, and so on. It records the donor’s row (donor_row), the level it matched at (level), and how many candidate donors that level offered (n_candidates). The result is a table called matched: panel plus those three columns. The block prints how many twins matched at each level, and the median number of candidates there.
Table 2.4. matched: twins per matching level, and the median number of candidate donors (median_cell).

THIN_CELL <- 5L
K <- list(
  function(d) paste(d$sexk, d$age_band, d$eth4, d$vote2024, d$educ2, sep = "|"),

hotdeck <- function(skel, pool, seed = 20260913L) {

  pick <- function(cand) if (length(cand) == 1L) cand else sample(cand, 1L)
  res <- rbindlist(lapply(seq_len(nrow(skel)), function(i) {
    for (lv in 1:5) {
      cand <- idx[[lv]][[key[[lv]][i]]]
      if (length(cand) >= THIN_CELL)
        return(data.table(donor_row = pick(cand), level = lv, n_candidates = length(cand)))
    }
    cand <- pool[age_band == skel$age_band[i], donor_row]    # last resort: age band only
    data.table(donor_row = pick(cand), level = 6L, n_candidates = length(cand))
  }))
  cbind(skel, res)

4. Render the persona
The twin’s half of the persona is written here: the civic record and the demographics. It follows the project’s persona template line for line. Two rules carry over from the project’s panel:

Every line says where it came from. A value labelled census frame cell; modelled was assigned from the skeleton’s frame cell; nobody reported it. A value labelled the matched survey respondent’s own answer is the donor’s.
For three fields, ethnicity, education and income, the donor’s own answer replaces the skeleton’s modelled value. In the project’s panel the skeleton is a voter-file row, and a value the file actually records is kept. A synthetic skeleton has no file row, so all of its values are modelled, and on these three fields the donor’s answer is the better information.

The civic record is where a synthetic twin differs most from a registrant twin. A registrant carries an observed turnout history from the voter file (2016 to 2024 generals, primary ballots, registration year). A synthetic skeleton has none, so the persona says so. It states 2024 turnout as modelled.
It never states the 2024 vote choice. Twin and donor share a 2024 vote class, because the class is a matching key, but the persona does not say what it is. The model has to work out the vote from the donor’s party, ideology and issue positions: that is Question A in Section 5.
The block below writes the persona as a function, render_persona(). It takes one skeleton (s) and its donor (d) and writes the text line by line: the civic record, the demographics (sex from the skeleton; ethnicity, education and income from the donor), then the donor’s donor_text. It runs the function for all 400 twins, storing each text in a new column of matched, persona_text, and checks that every persona contains its own donor’s text. It prints how many personas there are, their median length in characters, and how many are identical.
Table 2.8. The 400 personas: count, median length, duplicates.

fld <- function(label, v) if (is.na(v)) sprintf("- %s: (absent)", label) else sprintf("- %s: %s", label, v)

LABEL <- "the state of Ohio"

render_persona <- function(s, d) {
  voted <- if (s$vote2024 == "stay") "no" else "yes"
  paste(c("=== PROFILE ===",
    sprintf("The following is a record describing an adult citizen in %s. It describes who you are: your", LABEL),
    "civic record, your circumstances, your values and your political opinions. Each section states where the", "information comes from.", "",
    "-- CIVIC RECORD (not observed: synthetic skeleton drawn from the census frame, no voter-file record) --",
    fld("Congressional district", s$cd),
    sprintf("- Voted in the November 2024 general election: %s (modelled from the census frame)", voted),
    "- Earlier general elections, primary participation, registration: (not observed)", "",
    "-- DEMOGRAPHICS (census frame cell; modelled fields marked, respondent's own answers marked) --",
    fld("Age", s$age), fld("Sex", paste0(SEX[[s$gender]], " (census frame cell; modelled)")),
    if (!is.na(d$eth_ces)) fld("Ethnicity", d$eth_ces) else fld("Ethnicity", paste0(s$ethnicity, " (census frame cell; modelled)")),
    if (!is.na(d$educ_ces)) fld("Education", d$educ_ces)
    else fld("Education", paste0(if (s$educ2 == "degree") "College degree" else "No college degree", " (census frame cell; modelled)")),
    fld("Household income", d$income_ces),
    fld("Marital status", d$marital_ces), "",
    d$donor_text,
    "=== END OF PROFILE ==="), collapse = "\n")
}

5. The digital interview
This is the Talking to Machines PoSSUM vote module, here in R, with one call per twin and two questions:

A. Did this person vote in November 2024, and if so, with what probability for Harris, Trump or someone else?
B. In the November 2026 special election for U.S. Senate in Ohio, with what probability do they vote for Sherrod Brown, Jon Husted, someone else, or not at all?

The model answers as a third-person analyst reading the record, in probabilities, with no “not sure”, and returns JSON checked against a fixed schema. The prompts are the project’s word for word except where the system prompt describes the record. It says “one voter” rather than “one registered voter”, and no longer says the civic record comes “from the state voter file”, because here neither is true.
The block below sets up the interview and prints nothing. MODEL is the language model; API_URL is where requests go; SYSTEM is the system prompt, which tells the model its role; QUESTION is the two questions, added after each persona; and SCHEMA fixes the shape of the answer: a yes/no for voting in 2024, three probabilities for 2024 (harris, trump, other) and four for 2026 (dem, rep, other, no_vote).

MODEL <- "gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07"
BASE <- Sys.getenv("OPENAI_BASE_URL"); if (!nzchar(BASE)) BASE <- "https://api.openai.com/v1"   # on the workshop server, the course proxy
API_URL <- paste0(sub("/+$", "", BASE), "/chat/completions")
SYSTEM <- paste(
  "You are an experienced election analyst. You will be given the record of one voter: their civic record,",
  "demographics, and the values, party identification and issue positions of a survey respondent matched to them.",
  "Reason about how a person with this record would vote. Answer in the third person, as probabilities, never 'not sure'.",
  "Base the answer on the record only; do not assume anything about the campaigns beyond what is stated in the question.")
QUESTION <- paste0(
  "QUESTION A. In the November 2024 presidential election in Ohio, did this person cast a ballot (see the civic record), and if so, ",
  "what is the probability that they voted for Kamala Harris (Democrat), Donald Trump (Republican), or another candidate?\n",
  "QUESTION B. In the November 2026 special election for U.S. Senate in Ohio, the candidates are Sherrod Brown (Democrat) and ",
  "Jon Husted (Republican, incumbent). What is the probability that this person votes for the Democrat, ",
  "votes for the Republican, votes for someone else, or does not vote in that election? Weigh the person's own turnout history: ",
  "someone who has skipped recent general elections is unlikely to vote in a midterm.\n",
  "Return JSON only.")
probs <- function(...) list(type = "object", additionalProperties = FALSE, required = c(...),
                            properties = setNames(rep(list(list(type = "number")), length(c(...))), c(...)))
SCHEMA <- list(type = "object", additionalProperties = FALSE,
               required = c("voted_2024", "vote_2024", "vote_2026"),
               properties = list(voted_2024 = list(type = "boolean"),
                                 vote_2024  = probs("harris", "trump", "other"),
                                 vote_2026  = probs("dem", "rep", "other", "no_vote")))


Cached answers
Every twin in the seeded draw has already been interviewed once, and the answers come with the notebook. This section therefore runs offline, at no cost, with the same result for everyone. An answer is looked up by the twin and its donor. If you change the seed in Notebook 1 or here, your new twins will not be in the cache. With an API key they are interviewed live and saved to output/interviews_live.jsonl.
The next block defines the helper functions and prints nothing:

ask_vote_module() sends one persona with the questions to the model and returns its answer;
answer_key() builds each twin’s lookup key: twin id, donor’s survey year and donor’s respondent id;
norm() and flatten() turn one answer into a row of numbers, rescaling probabilities to add up to 1 (a few answers come back in percent);
read_answers() reads a file of answers into a table.


ask_vote_module <- function(persona_text) {
  body <- list(model = MODEL, reasoning_effort = "low",
               messages = list(list(role = "system", content = SYSTEM),
                               list(role = "user", content = paste0("RECORD:\n", persona_text, "\n\n", QUESTION))),
               response_format = list(type = "json_schema",
                                      json_schema = list(name = "vote_module", strict = TRUE, schema = SCHEMA)))
  resp <- httr2::request(API_URL) |>
    httr2::req_auth_bearer_token(Sys.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY")) |>
    httr2::req_body_json(body, auto_unbox = TRUE) |>
    httr2::req_retry(max_tries = 4) |>
    httr2::req_perform() |>
    httr2::resp_body_json()
  c(fromJSON(resp$choices[[1]]$message$content),
    list(model = MODEL, in_tok = resp$usage$prompt_tokens, out_tok = resp$usage$completion_tokens))
}

answer_key <- function(d) paste(d$twin_id, pool$donor_year[d$donor_row], pool$donor_caseid[d$donor_row], sep = "|")
norm <- function(p) { p <- unlist(p); if (sum(p) > 0) p / sum(p) else p }   # a few answers come back in percent
flatten <- function(a) { v24 <- norm(a$vote_2024); v26 <- norm(a$vote_2026)
  data.table(voted_2024_llm = a$voted_2024,
             harris = v24[["harris"]], trump = v24[["trump"]], other_2024 = v24[["other"]],
             dem = v26[["dem"]], rep = v26[["rep"]], other_2026 = v26[["other"]], no_vote = v26[["no_vote"]]) }
NO_ANSWERS <- data.table(answer_id = character(), voted_2024_llm = logical(), harris = numeric(), trump = numeric(), other_2024 = numeric(),
                         dem = numeric(), rep = numeric(), other_2026 = numeric(), no_vote = numeric())
read_answers <- function(f) if (file.exists(f)) rbindlist(lapply(readLines(f), function(l) { a <- fromJSON(l); cbind(data.table(answer_id = a$answer_id), flatten(a)) })) else NO_ANSWERS

The next block runs the interview. It reads the cached answers (data/oh_syn_interviews.jsonl) and any live ones, gives every twin in matched its lookup key, and counts how many twins already have an answer. Any twin without one is interviewed live, but only if an API key is set. Finally it joins the answers to the twins in a table called iv, one row per interviewed twin, and prints how many there are.
Text 2.3. The interview: answers found in the cache, and twins interviewed.

CACHE <- file.path(DATA, "oh_syn_interviews.jsonl")
LIVE  <- file.path(OUT, "interviews_live.jsonl")
all_answers <- function() { a <- rbindlist(list(NO_ANSWERS, read_answers(CACHE), read_answers(LIVE)), use.names = TRUE); if (!nrow(a)) return(NO_ANSWERS); unique(a, by = "answer_id") }
matched[, answer_id := answer_key(.SD)]

answers <- all_answers()
todo <- matched[!answer_id %in% answers$answer_id]
cat(sprintf("%d of %d twins answered from the cache; %d to interview\n",
            nrow(matched) - nrow(todo), nrow(matched), nrow(todo)))

400 of 400 twins answered from the cache; 0 to interview

if (nrow(todo) > 0 && nzchar(Sys.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"))) {
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(todo))) {
    a <- ask_vote_module(todo$persona_text[i])
    cat(toJSON(c(list(answer_id = todo$answer_id[i]), a), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = NA), "\n", file = LIVE, append = TRUE, sep = "")
  }
  answers <- all_answers()
}
iv <- merge(matched, answers, by = "answer_id")
cat(sprintf("%d twins interviewed\n", nrow(iv)))

400 twins interviewed


Text 2.3 should read “400 of 400 twins answered from the cache” and “400 twins interviewed”. Each row of iv is now a twin with its answers: harris, trump and other_2024 for 2024, and dem, rep, other_2026 and no_vote for 2026.

text:
2. The daily interview
Every trading day, each twin in the panel receives the same two messages:

a system prompt that tells the model whose shoes to step into and pastes in the profile card;
a user prompt with the rules of the survey, then one block per stock asking for a recommendation from 0 (a very strong sell) to 100 (a very strong buy), a confidence score, how speculative the answer is, an expected holding period, and the main catalyst.

The prompts below are the panel’s own, from its public code repository. The block loads them into prompts and prints where they come from.
Text 1.2. Source of the prompts.

prompts <- fromJSON(file.path(DATA, "ff_prompts.json"))
cat(prompts$source)

github.com/talking-to-machines/ai-population, ai_population/prompts/prompt_template.py (main, commit 5350584)


The panel’s system prompt also invites the model to search the web for up-to-date news about the stocks and themes the influencer cares about. That is what keeps a twin current, and it is also what anchors each answer in time: a twin interviewed on 3 September can find news up to 3 September and nothing later. Notebook 2 relies on that. It tests whether a twin’s view on day t predicts returns after day t, which is only fair if the twin could not see those returns.
The live interview in Section 3 has no web search, so the version used here drops that paragraph. The block below prints the system prompt as your twin will receive it.
Text 1.3. The system prompt, with twin TWIN’s card.

SYSTEM <- sub("{profile}", card_text(TWIN), prompts$system_workshop, fixed = TRUE)
cat(SYSTEM)

Please put yourself in the shoes of a X (formerly Twitter) financial influencer participating in a financial market survey. Your profile was previously evaluated by an LLM during an onboarding phase and determined to be a financial influencer focusing on stock trading and equities, bonds and fixed income, or options trading and derivatives, based on your past posts and profile information. As part of this survey:
1. Your profile and posts will be monitored daily
2. You will undergo daily interviews to discuss your perspective on the financial markets

Here are the details of the X (formerly Twitter) profile you will be analyzing:
- Profile ID: ff05
- Profile Description: Dividend investor and investing instructor; admirer of Warren Buffett; sells put options.
- Profile Creation Date: 2011
- Blue Verified Profile: TRUE
- Number of Followers: about 21,000 Followers
- Total Number of Tweets: about 48,000
- Main focus: Dividend growth stocks, with some options and trend trading
- Audience: Seasoned investors
- Recent posts (summarised):
  * Daily posts on long-standing dividend-raising companies
  * Celebrates a large gain on a chip-maker position from a trend-trading class account
  * Blue-chip, income-first tone

Instructions
Analyze the provided information and answer the following questions based strictly on:
- The X (formerly Twitter) profile details above.
Do not infer or assume any details beyond what is supported by this profile. If information is uncertain or conflicting, acknowledge this explicitly. Keep responses concise, precise, and data-driven.


The next block builds the user prompt for the 20 stocks of this notebook. The panel sends 50 stocks per message; 20 fit in one message comfortably. It prints the rules, then the block for the first stock.
Text 1.4. The user prompt: the rules and the first stock’s block.

slice <- fread(file.path(DATA, "ff_interviews_slice.csv"))
slice[, event_date := as.IDate(event_date)]
stocks <- unique(slice[, .(ticker, company)])[order(ticker)]
stocks[, label := sprintf("%s (%s)", company, ticker)]

blocks    <- vapply(stocks$label, function(s) sub("{stock}", s, prompts$stock_block, fixed = TRUE), "")
questions <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(stocks)), function(i)
  sub("{stock}", stocks$label[i], sub("{i}", i, prompts$stock_question, fixed = TRUE), fixed = TRUE), "")
USER <- paste0(prompts$user_prefix, paste(blocks, collapse = "\n\n"), prompts$must_answer,
               paste(questions, collapse = "\n\n"))
cat(prompts$user_prefix, blocks[1], sep = "")

You will be presented with a series of questions, each preceded by predefined response options labeled with a symbol (e.g. "A1", "A2", "B1", etc.).

For each question, follow these instructions strictly:
1) Select the most likely response based strictly on the provided profile data. The chosen response must be the most accurate representation of the profile.
2) For each question, indicate the level of speculation involved in your response on a scale from 0 (not speculative at all, every single element of the profile data was useful in the selection) to 100 (fully speculative, there is no information related to this question in the profile data). Speculation levels should be a direct measure of the amount of useful information available in the profile and pertain only to the information available in the profile data -- namely the username, name, description, profile picture, and videos from the profile-- and should not be affected by additional information available to you from any other source.

To ensure consistency, use the following guidelines to determine speculation levels:
0-20 (Low speculation): The profile data provides clear and direct information relevant to the question. (e.g., explicit mention in the profile or videos)
21-40 (Moderate-low speculation): The profile data provides indirect but strong indicators relevant to the question. (e.g., context from multiple sources within the profile or videos)
41-60 (Moderate speculation): The profile data provides some hints or partial information relevant to the question. (e.g., inferred from user interests or indirect references)
61-80 (Moderate-high speculation): The profile data provides limited and weak indicators relevant to the question. (e.g., very subtle hints or minimal context)
81-100 (High speculation): The profile data provides no or almost no information relevant to the question. (e.g., assumptions based on very general information)

3) When asked to provide an explanation, please provide a detailed explanation and the data features that contributed to your response.
4) When asked to provide a recommendation, please indicate on a scale of 0 to 100 your overall recommendation for a particular stock/stock ticker (0 means a very strong sell recommendation and 100 means a very strong buy recommendation). For example, a strong sell recommendation would be in the 0-20 range, a moderate sell recommendation would be in the 20-40 range, a hold recommendation would be in the 40-60 range, a moderate buy recommendation would be in the 60-80 range, and a strong buy recommendation would be 80+.
5) When asked to provide a confidence score, please indicate on a scale of 0 to 100 a measure of confidence for your stock pick (0-20 means low confidence, 20-40 means moderate-to-low confidence, 40-60 means moderate confidence, 60-80 means moderate-to-high confidence, and 80+ means high confidence).
6) When asked to provide an expected holding period (days), please indicate the time horizon (in days) over which you will hold a particular stock.
7) When asked to provide a primary catalyst type, please indicate the main factor you expect to drive the stock’s performance. You must select from the following options: Earnings, Macro, Product, Regulatory, Flow-Technical, or Other.
8) Preserve a strictly structured response format to ensure clarity and ease parsing of the text.

Required format: Enclose each line of your response between two asterisks (**) at the beginning and end. Each line must begin with the field name in lowercase, followed by a colon (:), and end with **. Do not include text outside the asterisks or additional lines.

**question: APPLE INC (AAPL)**
**explanation: [Detailed explanation for recommendation]**
**recommendation: [Value selected]**
**confidence: [Value selected]**  
**speculation: [Speculation score selected]**
**expected holding period: [Number of days selected]** 
**primary catalyst type: [Earnings/Macro/Product/Regulatory/Flow-Technical/Other]**


The answer comes back as lines like **recommendation: 70**. The next block defines parse_answer(), which turns that text into a table with one row per stock. It prints nothing.

parse_answer <- function(txt) {
  parts <- strsplit(txt, "\\*\\*question:", perl = TRUE)[[1]][-1]
  field <- function(p, f) {
    m <- regmatches(p, regexpr(paste0("\\*\\*", f, ":\\s*([^*]*)\\*\\*"), p, perl = TRUE))
    if (!length(m)) return(NA_character_)
    trimws(sub(paste0("^\\*\\*", f, ":\\s*"), "", sub("\\*\\*$", "", m)))
  }
  rbindlist(lapply(parts, function(p) {
    q <- sub("\\*\\*.*$", "", p)
    data.table(ticker         = sub(".*\\(([A-Z.]+)\\)\\s*$", "\\1", trimws(q)),
               recommendation = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(field(p, "recommendation"))),
               confidence     = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(field(p, "confidence"))),
               speculation    = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(field(p, "speculation"))),
               holding_days   = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(field(p, "expected holding period"))),
               catalyst       = field(p, "primary catalyst type"),
               explanation    = field(p, "explanation"))
  }))
}

title: Notebook 2 — A silicon audience: writing ads for five kinds of voter
text:
A silicon audience is a panel of digital twins: a language model, given one voter’s record, predicts how that voter would answer a question about a political message. The Talking to Machines group uses such panels to decide which message reaches which voter before the message runs, and it is testing the panels against the people they are built from in a pre-registered study (OSF, 7 October 2026).
In this notebook a language model writes a thirty-second television ad, and you improve the instructions it is given, in three stages. Every ad is aimed at one of five kinds of Ohio voter, from strong Democrats to strong Republicans, and every ad gets two scores:

Does it read like a real ad? Judges compare it with a real Ohio campaign ad and try to spot the machine-written one.
Does it hit its group? The twins say how likely they would be to vote for the candidate behind it, and the ad should do better with its own group than with the other four.

The sections, in about forty-five minutes:

The Voters: the 400 Ohio twins you built this morning, in five groups;
The question: your issue, and the one question every twin answers;
The study’s scripts: how the five groups rated the scripts in the pre-registered study, and how to read a score that is about aim;
Stage 1: a basic prompt writes five ads, one per group;
Stage 2: the same prompt with what our tests taught us added;
Stage 3: your prompt, run live: push the aim higher than Stage 2;
The leaderboard, and what the loop does next;
What a twin cannot know.

Stages 1 and 2, and one worked example of Stage 3, were run once by the organisers and ship with the notebook, so the same prompt gives everyone the same ads and the same scores. Only Stage 3 calls a language model, and only if an API key is set. Everything else runs offline from the files beside this notebook.

read_jsonl <- function(f) {

        others_ptv = round(mean(ptv[group != target[1]]), 2)), by = .(ad_id, target)][
    , aim := round(target_ptv - others_ptv, 2)][]

text:
4. Stage 1: the basic prompt
From here on a language model writes the ads. The factory is a single call to the workshop model with a prompt printed in full below: one prompt, one call, no hidden machinery. {issue} and {group} are filled in for each ad, so one prompt writes five ads, one per group.
The block below reads your key and the proxy address from the environment, defines the prompts and the model calls, and prints the Stage 1 prompt.

fill() puts the issue and the group into a prompt;
write_ads() sends a filled prompt for each group and returns the five ads. The workshop model sometimes declines to write a political ad aimed at a named group of voters (“Sorry, I can’t create targeted political persuasion…”); when it does, write_ads() asks again, up to three times, and column asked records how many tries each ad took. An ad still declined after three tries is marked declined and is not scored;
run_ads() puts each ad to the audience and to the judges (below).

Text 4.1. The Stage 1 prompt.

MODEL <- "gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07"
key   <- Sys.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY")
base  <- Sys.getenv("OPENAI_BASE_URL", unset = "https://api.openai.com/v1")
API   <- paste0(sub("/+$", "", base), "/chat/completions")

STAGE1 <- paste(
  "Write the script for a thirty-second television advertisement by a candidate running for office in Ohio.",
  "75 to 85 words, spoken by the candidate in the first person, ending with \"And I approve this message.\"",
  "Name no candidate, party or office. The advertisement is about {issue}. It should win the vote of {group} in Ohio.")
STAGE2_ADD <- paste(
  "Write it the way a real candidate speaks. Say once, flatly, what you did before politics that gives you the right",
  "to talk about this: a job, a service, a business. Put in one concrete scene or detail, a person, a street, a price,",
  "invented but with nobody named. Promise what you will do in plain verbs, naming the instrument, never \"fix\" or",
  "\"stand up to\". Short spoken sentences, contractions, no hedging, no balancing the other side, no neat parallel",
  "closing line.")
EXAMPLE_ADD <- "Mention one thing the voter can check for themselves."    # the worked example of Stage 3 (Section 6)

fill <- function(prompt, group) paste0(
  gsub("{group}", GROUPS$phrase[match(group, GROUPS$group)], gsub("{issue}", it$issue, prompt, fixed = TRUE), fixed = TRUE),
  "\n\nReturn the script only.")

chat <- function(messages, response_format = NULL) {
  body <- list(model = MODEL, reasoning_effort = "low", messages = messages)
  if (!is.null(response_format)) body$response_format <- response_format
  httr2::request(API) |> httr2::req_auth_bearer_token(key) |> httr2::req_body_json(body) |>
    httr2::req_retry(max_tries = 3) |> httr2::req_timeout(120)
}
perform_all <- function(reqs, workers = 8) {
  if (packageVersion("httr2") >= "1.1.0") httr2::req_perform_parallel(reqs, on_error = "continue", max_active = workers, progress = FALSE)
  else httr2::req_perform_parallel(reqs, pool = curl::new_pool(total_con = workers, host_con = workers), on_error = "continue", progress = FALSE)
}
content_of <- function(r) if (inherits(r, "error") || is.null(r)) NA_character_ else
  trimws(httr2::resp_body_json(r)$choices[[1]]$message$content)
n_words <- function(x) lengths(strsplit(x, "\\s+"))

is_ad <- function(x) !is.na(x) & grepl("approve this message", x, ignore.case = TRUE) &
  !grepl("^\\W*(sorry|i'm sorry|i am sorry|i can.?t|i cannot)", x, ignore.case = TRUE)

write_ads <- function(prompt, id_prefix, tries = 3) {    # asks again, up to `tries` times, for any ad the model declined
  text <- rep(NA_character_, nrow(GROUPS)); asked <- integer(nrow(GROUPS))
  for (t in seq_len(tries)) {
    todo <- which(!is_ad(text))
    if (!length(todo)) break
    reqs <- lapply(GROUPS$group[todo], function(g) chat(list(list(role = "user", content = fill(prompt, g)))))
    text[todo] <- vapply(perform_all(reqs), content_of, character(1)); asked[todo] <- t
  }
  data.table(ad_id = paste0(id_prefix, "_", GROUPS$group), issue = it$key, target = GROUPS$group,
             prompt = prompt, text = text, asked = asked, declined = !is_ad(text))[, words := n_words(text)][]
}

cat(strwrap(STAGE1, width = 90), sep = "\n")

Write the script for a thirty-second television advertisement by a candidate running for
office in Ohio. 75 to 85 words, spoken by the candidate in the first person, ending with
"And I approve this message." Name no candidate, party or office. The advertisement is
about {issue}. It should win the vote of {group} in Ohio.



The audience and the judges
Four hundred twins is more than a live round needs. The next block draws the audience for every ad in Stages 1 to 3: ten twins from each group, fifty in all, with a fixed seed so that everyone in the room scores on the same fifty.
It also loads the real ads: ten thirty-second campaign spots, nine from Ohio and one from Illinois, taken from Google’s political-ad archive with the candidates’ names removed (five Republican, five Democratic). They are what the judges compare each machine-written ad with. Each ad is shown to forty judges, separate calls to the same model, each with one real ad, and each judge is asked which of the two is the real one. Every machine-written ad meets each of the ten real ads four times: twice with the real ad shown first (text A) and twice with it shown second (text B). The order matters because the judges lean towards text A, and showing each pairing both ways means that lean weighs the same on every ad. An ad’s spotted score is the share of its judges who picked the real ad correctly: 0.5 is what guessing gives, so an ad near 0.5 or below reads like a real one, and 1 means every judge saw through it. An ad passes if at least one judge was fooled.
The block prints the judge’s instruction, and one real ad so you can hear what the judges hear.
Text 4.2. The judge’s instruction, and one of the real ads.

set.seed(2026)
audience <- panel[!is.na(group), .SD[sample(.N, 10)], by = group]
real_ads <- read_jsonl(file.path(DATA, "real_ads_judges.jsonl"))
N_JUDGES <- 40

JUDGE <- paste(
  "You are shown two texts. Each is the spoken words of a thirty-second American political advertisement.",
  "One of them is a real advertisement that a candidate's campaign put on the air. The other was written",
  "by a machine imitating one. Names have been removed from both.\nSay which one is the real advertisement.\n",
  "Return only: {\"real\": \"A\" or \"B\", \"confidence\": <50-100>}")
JUDGE_SCHEMA <- list(type = "object", additionalProperties = FALSE, required = c("real", "confidence"),
                     properties = list(real = list(type = "string", enum = list("A", "B")),
                                       confidence = list(type = "integer", minimum = 50, maximum = 100)))

twin_request <- function(persona_text, script) chat(
  list(list(role = "system", content = HEADER),
       list(role = "user", content = paste0("=== PROFILE ===\n", persona_text, "\n=== END OF PROFILE ===\n\n", question_block(script)))),
  response_format = list(type = "json_schema", json_schema = list(name = "ptv", strict = TRUE, schema = SCHEMA)))
judge_pairs <- function(id) {                # every real ad in both slots, A and B; the same draw for the same ad, every run
  set.seed(sum(utf8ToInt(id) * seq_along(utf8ToInt(id))))
  grid <- CJ(ref_id = real_ads$ref_id, real_pos = c("A", "B"))
  grid <- grid[rep(seq_len(.N), ceiling(N_JUDGES / .N))][sample(.N)][seq_len(N_JUDGES)]
  data.table(ad_id = id, judge = seq_len(N_JUDGES), grid)
}
judge_request <- function(machine, real, real_pos) chat(
  list(list(role = "user", content = paste0(JUDGE, "\n\nText A:\n", if (real_pos == "A") real else machine,
                                            "\n\nText B:\n", if (real_pos == "A") machine else real))),
  response_format = list(type = "json_schema", json_schema = list(name = "judge", strict = TRUE, schema = JUDGE_SCHEMA)))

run_ads <- function(ads) {                   # ads: ad_id, text. 50 twins + 40 judges per ad, all in parallel
  tw <- CJ(ad = seq_len(nrow(ads)), k = seq_len(nrow(audience)))
  jp <- rbindlist(lapply(ads$ad_id, judge_pairs))
  reqs <- c(lapply(seq_len(nrow(tw)), function(r) twin_request(audience$persona_text[tw$k[r]], ads$text[tw$ad[r]])),
            lapply(seq_len(nrow(jp)), function(r) judge_request(ads[ad_id == jp$ad_id[r], text],
                                                                real_ads[ref_id == jp$ref_id[r], text], jp$real_pos[r])))
  resps <- perform_all(reqs)
  failed <- vapply(resps, function(r) inherits(r, "error") || is.null(r), logical(1))
  first_error <- if (any(failed)) conditionMessage(resps[[which(failed)[1]]]) else NA_character_
  out <- vapply(resps, content_of, character(1))
  t_out <- out[seq_len(nrow(tw))]; j_out <- out[nrow(tw) + seq_len(nrow(jp))]
  answers <- tw[, .(ad_id = ads$ad_id[ad], twin_id = audience$twin_id[k], persona_sha256 = audience$persona_sha256[k],
                    ptv = vapply(t_out, function(x) if (is.na(x)) NA_real_ else as.numeric(fromJSON(x)$ptv), numeric(1)),
                    model = MODEL)][!is.na(ptv)]
  jp[, `:=`(pick = vapply(j_out, function(x) if (is.na(x)) NA_character_ else fromJSON(x)$real, character(1)),
            confidence = vapply(j_out, function(x) if (is.na(x)) NA_real_ else as.numeric(fromJSON(x)$confidence), numeric(1)),
            model = MODEL)]
  jp[, spotted := pick == real_pos]
  list(answers = answers, judges = jp[!is.na(pick)], failed = sum(failed), first_error = first_error)
}
scoreboard <- function(ads, answers, judges) {
  a <- aim(group_means(answers), ads)
  s <- judges[, .(judges = .N, spotted = round(mean(spotted), 2)), by = ad_id]
  d <- merge(merge(ads[, .(ad_id, target)], a[, .(ad_id, target_ptv, others_ptv, aim)], by = "ad_id"), s, by = "ad_id")
  d[, passes := spotted < 1][order(match(target, GROUPS$group))]
}
five_bars <- function(ads, answers) {
  gm <- merge(group_means(answers), ads[, .(ad_id, target)], by = "ad_id")
  gm[, panel := paste("written for", GROUPS$label[match(target, GROUPS$group)])]
  gm[, panel := factor(panel, levels = paste("written for", GROUPS$label))]
  ggplot(gm, aes(x = factor(group, levels = GROUPS$group), y = ptv, fill = group, alpha = group == target)) +
    geom_col() + facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1, labeller = label_wrap_gen(16)) +
    scale_fill_manual(NULL, values = GROUP_COLOURS, guide = "none") +
    scale_alpha_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 1, `FALSE` = 0.35), guide = "none") +
    scale_x_discrete(NULL) + scale_y_continuous("Mean vote likelihood, 0-10", limits = c(0, 10)) +
    theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7))
}
spotted_adjusted <- function(sbs, judges) {  # each ad and each prompt pooled, with real ad x slot fixed effects
  key <- rbindlist(lapply(names(sbs), function(n) sbs[[n]][, .(ad_id, prompt = n, target)]))
  j <- merge(judges[, .(ad_id, ref_id, real_pos, spotted = as.numeric(spotted))], key, by = "ad_id")
  j[, cell := interaction(ref_id, real_pos)]
  est <- function(unit) {                    # unit means at the average real ad and slot, and their 95% intervals
    s <- coef(summary(lm(as.formula(paste("spotted ~ 0 +", unit, "+ cell")), data = j, contrasts = list(cell = "contr.sum"))))
    s <- s[startsWith(rownames(s), unit), , drop = FALSE]
    data.table(id = sub(paste0("^", unit), "", rownames(s)), spotted = s[, 1], lo = s[, 1] - 1.96 * s[, 2], hi = s[, 1] + 1.96 * s[, 2])
  }
  rbind(merge(key, est("ad_id"), by.x = "ad_id", by.y = "id")[, .(prompt, target, spotted, lo, hi)],
        est("prompt")[, .(prompt = id, target = "ALL", spotted, lo, hi)])
}
spotted_bars <- function(sbs, judges) {      # sbs: named list of scoreboards, one per prompt, drawn left to right
  d <- spotted_adjusted(sbs, judges)
  d[, prompt := factor(prompt, levels = names(sbs))]
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.8)
  ggplot(d, aes(x = factor(target, levels = c(GROUPS$group, "ALL")), y = spotted, fill = target, alpha = prompt, group = prompt)) +
    geom_col(position = dodge, width = 0.75) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), position = dodge, width = 0.25, alpha = 1, colour = "grey20") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 5.5, colour = "grey70") +
    scale_fill_manual(NULL, values = c(GROUP_COLOURS, ALL = "#333333"), guide = "none") +
    scale_alpha_manual(NULL, values = seq(0.35, 1, length.out = length(sbs))) +
    scale_x_discrete("Ad written for", labels = c(GROUPS$group, "All five\npooled")) +
    scale_y_continuous("Spotted: share of judges who picked the real ad", breaks = seq(0.25, 1, 0.25)) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.25, 1)) +
    theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "top")
}

Note to Figure 5.2. Each bar is a share of judge calls: of the 40 calls for one ad, or the 200 for the five pooled, the share in which the judge picked the real ad. Much of the noise in that share has a known source. Which real ad a judge saw, and whether it was shown first or second, moves the chance of a correct pick more than anything else: some real ads are picked almost every time when shown first and almost never when shown second. Every machine-written ad meets the same real ads in the same slots, so this does not favour any ad, and the intervals take it out. They come from a linear regression of each call’s spotted (1 if the judge picked the real ad, 0 if not) on one indicator for each ad, or for each stage in the pooled bars, and one fixed effect for each pairing of real ad and slot (A or B), coded to sum to zero; because every ad meets each pairing equally often, each ad’s coefficient is exactly its share. The intervals are the coefficient plus and minus 1.96 standard errors, with the residual variance pooled over all the calls in the figure, so every ad’s interval has the same width. They take the ads as given: they measure how much a share would move with another set of judges for these ads, not the larger variation that would come from the model writing a different ad from the same prompt. Whether the Stage 2 prompt would also beat Stage 1 with five other ads is a question only more ads can answer.

text:
8. What a twin cannot know
Three things to carry out of the room.
The twin answers from a persona built from a census cell and a matched survey respondent’s own answers. It has never seen an advertisement rated by that respondent, and it was told nothing about this study. When an ad scores well, you can read the persona and see why; when it scores badly, the same.
Whether the twins’ ratings match those of the people they are built from is an open question, and the group is answering it the only way that counts: a pre-registered study (OSF, DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/CKAM2, 7 October 2026) in which each human respondent rates the fifteen scripts of Section 3 on four questions, and the model predicts that person’s answers from their profile. Today you asked one of those questions, vote likelihood, about ads a model wrote to your instructions. Until the humans have answered, a leaderboard is a leaderboard of twins. The judges are a model too: a judge may recognise a real ad from memory, which works against you, and a human viewer may spot habits the judges miss.
And a choice worth noticing: this morning’s vote module asked the model to estimate probabilities about a record, as an analyst; this afternoon the model predicted the answer a particular person would give, on the scale that person sees. They are different instruments, and a method that cannot say which it used is not a method. The registered study uses the second.
